blocks.heading: That squeaky-clean feeling is a bad sign, not a good one
quotes: “My face felt tight afterwards and I took that to mean clean.”
“Oily skin, so I washed four times a day. It only got oilier.”
“I upgraded to an expensive serum and my skin still stung. The problem was the wash.”
“Hot water feels good, and by winter I was flaking around my nose.”

explainer.heading: A step repeated 730 times a year multiplies whatever it gets wrong
body: Skin holds water in behind a thin layer of oil and ceramides. A harsh surfactant strips that layer along with the dirt — and the tight, squeaky feeling is the moment it comes off.
Skin answers by producing more oil. Which is why washing more often because your skin is oily usually makes it oilier, not less.

This bottle states four absences on the pack — no sulfates, no alcohol, no parabens, no silicones — and puts Ceramide and Pro-vitamin B5 into the step that takes things away. Nothing miraculous about it. The step you repeat most in a day is simply worth getting right.

blocks.transition: If how your skin feels afterwards is the wrong measure, the right one is in the ingredient table below.

blocks.heading: Three skin types, three different ways to use it
blocks.intro: Same bottle, but frequency and water temperature should differ. This is the part most often skipped.

items.heading: Oily skin, visible pores
items.body: Twice a day, no more. A third wash starts taking away more than the skin can replace, and the oil-rebound cycle begins there.

items.heading: Dry or thin skin
items.body: Cleanser at night, cool water alone in the morning. Your skin does not collect enough overnight to justify another round of surfactant.

items.heading: Skin that is flaking badly or stinging
items.body: With a damaged barrier, every cleansing step makes it worse. Stop strong actives, use cool water for a few days, and see a doctor if it does not settle.

blocks.heading: Four actives printed on the bottle, and four things left out
blocks.intro: A good cleanser is judged by what it does not do: no tightness, no stripped feeling afterwards.

rows.name: Pro-vitamin B5 (panthenol)
rows.role: Humectant, aimed at reducing the tight feeling after washing.

rows.name: Nano-ceramide
rows.role: Ceramide at nano scale; ceramides are a building block of the skin barrier.

rows.name: Lactobacillus ferment
rows.role: Fermented ingredient, related to the skin surface microbiome.

rows.name: Hydroxyethyl urea
rows.role: Humectant that holds water in the outer layer.

rows.name: Sulfate-free
rows.role: Strong foaming agents, often linked to the stripped feeling after washing.

rows.name: Alcohol-free

rows.name: Silicone-free

blocks.eyebrow: Where it sits in the day
blocks.heading: The first step, and the one that decides whether the rest absorb
blocks.intro: Everything applied afterwards goes onto skin you have just washed. Wash it wrong and the later steps pay for it.

steps.label: Wet with cool water
steps.note: Hot water strips natural oils faster than any active in the bottle replaces them.

steps.label: Lather in your hands first
steps.note: Work it up before it touches your face. Rubbing unlathered cleanser on skin is rubbing with a paste.

steps.label: Rinse, then blot with a soft towel
steps.note: Blot, do not rub. Apply the next step while the skin is still slightly damp rather than waiting for it to dry.

steps.label: Remove make-up first
steps.note: Sunscreen and make-up are not water-soluble, so a cleanser alone will not lift all of it.

steps.label: Then cleanse
steps.note: This step takes the rest, plus the day's excess oil.

steps.label: Blot dry and move on to treatment
steps.note: Do not let the skin dry out completely first.

blocks.footnote: Twice a day suits most people. After sport or a dusty day outside, an extra wash is reasonable — but do not let it become a daily habit.

blocks.heading: Three steps, morning and night
blocks.intro: At night, if you wore make-up or sunscreen, remove that first and then do this step.

items.heading: Wet your face with cool water
items.body: Hot water removes more natural oil than needed and leaves the skin tight.

items.heading: Lather in your palms first
items.body: Build the lather before it reaches your face; rubbing unlathered product on skin is friction you do not need.

items.heading: Rinse and blot dry
items.body: Blot with a clean towel, do not rub. Apply the next step while the skin is still slightly damp.

blocks.footnote: Twice a day is enough. Washing more often does not make skin cleaner, it only thins the barrier.

blocks.heading: Do you need both micellar water and a cleanser?
blocks.intro: Short answer: at night yes, in the morning no. The table says why.

criteria.label: What it lifts

blocks.footnote: People who wear no make-up still need to remove sunscreen — and if you are working on melasma or dark marks then sunscreen is not a step you skip, so the removal step comes with it.

Sulfates are strong foaming agents; more foam does not mean cleaner. A sulfate-free formula foams less, and that is normal rather than a sign of a weak product.

items.q: Do I need a make-up remover first?
items.a: Yes, if there is make-up or sunscreen on your skin. A face wash alone often does not lift sunscreen fully, and the residue is a common cause of congestion.

items.q: Can I use it during a pigmentation routine?
items.a: It is the cleansing step of that routine — step one in the morning and step two at night. That is why it comes with the combo.
Keep away from heat and direct sunlight, close the cap after use, keep out of reach of children. Avoid contact with the eyes; if it gets in, rinse immediately with clean water.
